extracted.intended_audience: public health researchers, health agency communications staff, science communication professionals, policy makers, and health journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria about preparing and issuing press releases (PRs) for health research evidence reports, and how PR content affects traditional media coverage. Focus is on accuracy, framing, dissemination and engagement during a public health emergency (COVID-19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and unbiased language in PRs
rubrics_metrics.description: “The content and language in these PRs must be accurate and unbiased as the content within a PR itself represents a large portion of the content of news stories.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality PRs issued by medical journals seem to increase the quality of associated newspaper coverage, whereas low-quality PRs might make them worse. Low-quality PRs can amplify reporting errors, overemphasize beneficial effects, or exaggerate study findings. Draft PR language to reflect study findings faithfully and avoid introducing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: State clear key messages/main points
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs should present the principal 'key messages' (main points) from each research report so media coverage reflects the intended findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study team developed explicit key messages from reports to code media coverage; where PRs omit individual study findings (as PR1 did), coverage may focus on organisational roles rather than results. Include concise, accurate key messages aligned to report findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include quotes from researchers in PRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing researcher quotes in PRs is valuable: “When researchers were quoted, it was largely sourced from quotes provided in the PR. This may have contributed to better reporting in our case and the use of quote in PRs may be helpful in disseminating accurate information to journalists.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply clear, contextualised quotes from named researchers to increase the likelihood that media will convey accurate interpretations; ensure quotes include caveats/uncertainty where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure balanced inclusion of perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs should facilitate media reports that include multiple perspectives: political, public health, and researchers, to support balanced reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly with human-interest coverage there can be tension between enthusiastic political/public responses and cautious public health experts. Efforts should be made to ensure all perspectives are included within a media report to ensure balanced reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective reporting and variable quoting that changes context
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective reporting and variability in the use of quotes from governmental and public health stakeholders can change and contextualise results in ways not intended by researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft PRs to minimise opportunities for selective quotation that could alter meaning; highlight the most critical findings and their limits so selective extracts are less likely to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour and accuracy in health-research PRs
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs require rigour and accuracy to prevent downstream misrepresentation: “This emphasises the need for rigour and accuracy in health research related PRs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure factual correctness, correct interpretation of statistics, and alignment with the underlying report methods and conclusions. Rigour reduces misrepresentation and amplification of errors in media coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate uncertainty and evidence limitations (include caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs should clearly communicate limitations, evidence quality, and uncertainty so news coverage does not overstate certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many underlying reports were of limited or low–moderate quality; PRs should explicitly note these limitations (eg, small samples, lack of peer review, inconsistent findings) and include caveats about what is not known to discourage unwarranted extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration and overemphasis of benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs must not overstate benefits or certainty: “Low quality PRs can result in media coverage that ... overemphasizes the beneficial effects of treatment, or generally over exaggerates study findings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautious, accurately worded headlines and summaries; avoid sensational language and ensure claims match the evidence strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disseminate technical reports as well as human-interest findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Make efforts to increase dissemination of technical reports: “media coverage appeared to focus more on ‘human-interest’ reports ... as opposed to those that were more technical … More efforts should be made to increase dissemination of technical reports, especially given the public’s need for factual scientific information in a pandemic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance accessible human-interest framing with clear routes to technical detail (links, summaries, FAQs) so journalists and specialists can access the full evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and multi-channel dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: PR timing and channels affect uptake: PRs were sent by email, published on the agency website, and promoted on social media; coverage was overwhelmingly reported on the day of and day after PR publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disseminate PRs promptly through multiple channels (email to media lists, website, social platforms) and coordinate timing to maximise accurate and timely coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide transparent links to original reports and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs should link to the full publicly available reports and reference methodological guidance to allow verification and deeper reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including direct links and methodological notes increases transparency and helps journalists accurately interpret and contextualise findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage proactively with journalists to facilitate accurate reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Better engagement with journalists is needed: PRs alone may be insufficient and journalists are indirect sources of public education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer interviews, expert availability, clarifying materials, and briefing notes to help journalists understand limitations and avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate messaging to avoid conflicting signals from actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting statements from political actors and public health specialists can create public confusion (example: optimistic political framing vs cautious CMO statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRs and communications should aim to clarify where evidence is tentative and encourage consistent messaging among policy-makers and experts, or explicitly explain differing interpretations and their bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: State policy implications carefully and transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: When implying policy relevance, PRs should present implications for policy makers while making clear the evidence base and limits: decisions cannot be based solely on single estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting tentative findings as definitive grounds for policy change; clearly state what the evidence does and does not support and recommend further monitoring where appropriate.
